name: Question & Answer
format:
Q: [An ordinary question]
A: [An unexpected answer]
example:
Q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
A: In a mirror, probably.
tip: Keep the question plain so the answer does all the work.

name: Teacher & Student
format:
Teacher: [A classroom question]
Student: [A literal or cheeky answer]
example:
Teacher: Name two days that start with T.
Student: Today and Tomorrow.
tip: The student is technically right, just not in the way the teacher meant.

name: Doctor & Patient
format:
Patient: Doctor, [a strange problem]
Doctor: [A practical reply]
Patient: [A twist]
example:
Patient: Doctor, I feel invisible.
Doctor: Next, please!
tip: Doctors deliver the punchline best when they stay completely calm.

name: Husband & Wife
format:
Wife/Husband: [A simple household question]
Husband/Wife: [A clever dodge or reversal]
example:
Wife: I'm going to my mother's!
Husband: Shall I book the ticket?
Wife: ...Now I'm definitely not going.
tip: Keep it affectionate. The best couple jokes laugh with both people.

name: Friend Conversation
format:
Friend: [A request or promise]
Me: [A reply]
Friend: [A twist that reveals the truth]
example:
Friend: I'll text you when I leave home.
Translation: I haven't woken up yet.
tip: Borrowed money, late arrivals and secrets are reliable setups.

name: Office Conversation
format:
Boss/HR: [A work question]
Employee: [An answer that is honest in the wrong way]
example:
Boss: You're late again.
Employee: My alarm had a meeting with the snooze button, and it ran long.
tip: Everyone recognises meetings, Mondays and mute buttons.

name: School Conversation
format:
Principal/Friend: [A question about school life]
Student: [An excuse with its own logic]
example:
Principal: Why were you sleeping in class?
Student: The teacher said, "Close your eyes and imagine the answer." I imagined too far.
tip: Quote the teacher's own words back as the excuse.

name: Family Conversation
format:
Mom/Dad/Grandparent: [A familiar family line]
Kid: [A reply]
Mom/Dad: [The reveal]
example:
Mom: I'll count to three. One... two...
Son: What happens at three?
Mom: Nobody has ever reached it.
tip: Use lines every family says, then flip them.

name: One-Liner
example: I'm reading a book about anti-gravity. I can't put it down.
tip: Put the funniest word as close to the end as possible.

name: Knock-Knock
format:
Knock knock.
Who's there?
[Word]
[Word] who?
[A pun built on the word]
example:
Knock knock.
Who's there?
Boo.
Boo who?
Don't cry, it's only a joke!
tip: Say the pun out loud before you share it. If it sounds right, it works.

name: Funny Dialogue
format:
Person A: [Line]
Person B: [Line]
Person A: [Line]
Person B: [Punchline]
example:
Boyfriend: Where do you want to eat?
Girlfriend: Anywhere.
Boyfriend: Pizza?
Girlfriend: No.
Boyfriend: So anywhere except everywhere?
tip: Use a rhythm of three before the punchline.

name: Funny Story
format:
[A short situation in 2–3 sentences]
[A small reveal that changes the meaning]
example: Santa sat in front of his new fridge for ten minutes every day. Banta asked what he was doing. Santa said, "Waiting to see when the light goes off."
tip: Cut every sentence that doesn't lead to the reveal.

name: Setup + Punchline
format:
[Setup that creates an expectation]
[Punchline that breaks it]
example:
Why do fish live in salt water?
Because pepper makes them sneeze.
tip: The setup should sound like a real question.

name: Short Joke
format: Two short lines: a situation and a twist.
example: My boss told me to have a good day. So I went home.
tip: Under 160 characters fits nicely in a status.

name: Long Joke
example:
Son: Dad, are bugs good to eat?
Dad: Not at the dinner table, please.
After dinner:
Dad: So, what did you want to ask?
Son: Never mind. There was one in your soup, but it's gone now.
tip: Each exchange should raise the stakes a little.
